strengths: Significant practical contribution: 40x speedup with 30% tighter intervals over Gibbs et al. (2023), addressing real computational bottleneck
Novel algorithmic approach: Elegant solution-path algorithm exploiting piecewise-linear structure in λ and S, avoiding repeated full optimizations
Principled high-dimensional extension: Well-motivated integration of low-rank latent embeddings with proper handling of symmetric computation requirement
Solid theoretical framework: Theorems 1-2 appropriately adapt to latent space; Assumptions 1-2 are reasonable; error analysis (Lemmas 7-10) is thorough
Comprehensive experiments: Diverse applications (synthetic, molecular, text, medical) with multiple baselines and detailed metrics
Reproducibility: Code released as Python package; detailed algorithmic descriptions enable reproduction
Honest limitations discussion: Section 4 appropriately acknowledges limitations (fixed α, unweighted quantile loss) without overclaiming
weaknesses: Weakened coverage guarantees in latent space: Theorem 1's error term E[∑υ̂ψ*_W]/E[ψ*_W] is unbounded in principle; paper claims it's 'measurable' but provides no bounds, magnitudes, or guidance on when small—concerning for stated conditional validity
Coverage guarantee gaps under embedding error: Lemma 10 shows error depends on embedding perturbation Δ(w'), which could be substantial in high dimensions, but no empirical estimates provided

Inconsistent theoretical treatment: Theorem 1 vs 2 have different assumptions (i.i.d. vs exchangeability, density kernel requirement); implications unclear. Assumption 3-4 for Proposition 4 are stronger than original Gibbs et al. but not discussed in main text

Concerning experimental results: ArXiv ML topic achieves 0.730 ± 0.34 coverage (target 0.90)—far from nominal with high variance; no diagnostic analysis of failure mode. Standard deviations sometimes large (up to 0.34), raising robustness questions

Limited scalability and complexity analysis: Largest calibration n=2400; no scaling analysis to n=50K+. Expected |E| and number of events not analyzed; claimed O((|E|+d)³) with |E|≪n but no empirical validation

Algorithm initialization and tuning: λ¹ initialization (Eq. 39) appears ad-hoc with arbitrary j* choice; sensitivity not analyzed. Hyperparameter grid for γ not specified; sensitivity to resolution unexplored

Presentation and clarity: Dense notation in Sections 2.1.2-2.1.3 reduces accessibility. Important results (Lemmas 3-4) relegated to appendix. Distinction between path existence and efficient computation could be clearer
Incomplete experimental details: Missing specifics on random seeds, pLSI convergence criteria, kernel matrix conditioning effects. No ablation studies on λ vs S paths or different kernel choices

Gap between claimed and actual guarantees: Shift from P(Y∈Ĉ|X) to P(Y∈Ĉ|π̂(X)) acknowledged as 'different notion of conditional coverage' but implications not fully explored; represents meaningful weakening

strengths: Addresses genuine computational bottleneck in Gibbs et al. [2023] with impressive 40× speedup
Sound technical contribution with clean piecewise-affine path-tracing formulation (Propositions 1-2)
Well-motivated extension to high-dimensional settings using low-rank latent embeddings
Comprehensive experiments across diverse domains (synthetic, molecules, text, medical imaging) with consistent coverage improvements
Good reproducibility practices: code released and detailed algorithmic descriptions in appendices
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: λ-path and S-path directly extend Li et al. [2007]; core path-tracing technique is well-established in optimization literature

Theoretical guarantees substantially weaker than presented: Theorem 1 provides kernel-reweighted localized coverage, not true conditional coverage; coverage gap term E[∑υ̂ψ*_W]/E[ψ*_W] is problem-dependent and hard to estimate
Theorem 2 requires strong alignment condition (T̂(X)=T(X) a.s.) with restrictive margin requirement; applicability unclear in practice

Empirical coverage improvements are marginal: SpeedCP ~0.88-0.92 vs SplitCP ~0.87-0.93 (both targeting 0.9); large error bars suggest differences often within noise; no statistical significance testing
Experimental baselines limited: SplitCP is unfair comparison (lacks latent structure); missing comparisons with other recent conditional CP methods or simpler linear alternatives
Method complexity not clearly justified: multiple hyperparameters (γ, λ, K) with limited selection guidance; initialization of λ (Section B.3.3) appears ad hoc; practical implementation error-prone

Presentation obscures key limitations: high-dimensional extension requires symmetric computation of π̂(·) across calibration+test (potential data leakage); fixed α for all test points; scalar regression only; practical applicability to simpler settings (p small) unclear

Embedding robustness analysis incomplete: Lemma 10 bounds have uncontrolled terms; no concrete rates or empirical validation of when alignment condition (Eq. 11) holds; Assumption 3 on population strong convexity added late in appendix
Synthetic experiments artificially favor adaptive methods: test points concentrated at simplex vertices while calibration symmetric; no ablation studies on design choices
Missing ablation studies: sensitivity to kernel choice, bandwidth γ, dimension K not analyzed; no investigation of when SpeedCP's complexity is justified vs simpler approaches

strengths: Significant practical improvement: 40× speedup over CondCP with 30% shorter intervals, making RKHS conformal prediction deployable at scale
Elegant algorithmic contribution: piecewise-linearity of solutions (Propositions 1-2) is well-exploited via path-tracing with elbow set |E| ≪ n
Comprehensive theoretical analysis: extends to exchangeability, provides finite-sample guarantees with explicit coverage gap characterization, careful treatment of embedding error
Thoughtful high-dimensional extension: proper motivation for low-rank embeddings (signal-to-noise), log-ratio transformation for compositional data, connection to admixture models (Theorem 2)
Extensive experimental validation: four diverse settings, consistent improvements in coverage uniformity, competitive interval lengths, clear partitioned evaluation strategy
Strong reproducibility: 38-page appendix with detailed proofs, algorithms, experimental protocols; code promised
Well-executed combination of ideas: while building on existing work (Li et al. 2007, Gibbs et al. 2023), the application and integration is novel and effective
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: λ-path extends Li et al. [2007] directly, S-path is conceptually similar, conformal framework from Gibbs et al. [2023]—primarily algorithmic engineering rather than conceptual breakthrough

Approximate theoretical guarantees: Theorem 1 provides coverage only on kernel-reweighted distribution, not true conditional P(Y ∈ Ĉ|X); coverage gap term lacks explicit bounds and is not empirically estimated

Unvalidated embedding assumptions: Theorem 2 requires T̂(X) = T(X) a.s. with margin condition (Lemma 9) that is never empirically verified on real datasets; finite-sample behavior under misspecification unclear

Incomplete hyperparameter guidance: kernel bandwidth γ selected by grid search with no sensitivity analysis; choice of Φ*(X) shown to affect coverage (Appendix D.1) but no a priori selection guidance; limited discussion of latent dimension K

Experimental limitations: modest dataset scales (n ≈ 1000-5000), no truly high-dimensional experiments (p in thousands), CondCP excluded from some comparisons due to computational issues, binary classification only in MRI setting

Practical guidance unclear: when is SpeedCP preferable to much faster SplitCP? Trade-off between complexity and coverage improvement not clearly articulated; multiple component orchestration (embeddings, γ grid, CV) underexplained

Incomplete empirical analysis: embedding estimation error impact in high dimensions (p ≫ n) not thoroughly studied; coverage gap estimation (Prop. 4) presented as contribution but utility not demonstrated; missing ablation studies
